title: content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string (lastmile-ai/mcp-agent)
raw_text:
content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string — open-source issue in lastmile-ai/mcp-agent. Labels: bug, good first issue. use home assistant as mcp server,  then Calling OpenAI ChatCompletion with messages,  but the content in message is a list structure.

OpenAI API Specification：
- content can only be a string or null.
- It cannot be a list, object, or any other type.

If content is a list,  some LLM(deepseek) return the following error:
`[mcp_agent.workflows.llm.augmented_llm_openai] Error: Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: messages[2]: invalid type: sequence, expected a string at line 1
summary: This open-source issue points out a common problem when interacting with large language model (LLM) APIs, specifically OpenAI's ChatCompletion. It highlights that the `content` field within the `messages` parameter is sometimes being sent as a list, but the OpenAI API specification clearly states it should be a string or null. When this data type mismatch occurs, some LLMs, like DeepSeek, will return an error, causing your application to fail. This matters because robust AI applications require precise adherence to API documentation. Understanding and correctly implementing API specifications is fundamental for reliable integration with various LLM providers. As a takeaway, always double-check the expected data types and formats in API documentation, and consider contributing to such "good first issues" to gain practical experience.

title: Grading the Grader: Lessons from Evaluating an Agentic Data Analysis System
author: Tian Zheng, Kai-Tai Hsu
raw_text: Agentic data analysis systems produce rich outputs, including code, numerical results, and verbal diagnostics. This makes them more challenging to evaluate than single-turn LLM responses. It is therefore necessary to distinguish genuine disagreement between an agent's output and a ground-truth answer from grading artifacts. We investigate how reliably automated graders assess such a system and what strategies improve grading quality by applying LAMBDA, a multi-agent data-analysis system, on 153 numerical QRData tasks from DSGym. We develop and evaluate a three-layer human-AI grading cascade: strict regex matching, LLM-based lenient grading, and snippet-based human inspection, which combines non-GenAI and GenAI strategies with different failure profiles. Both automated graders achieve 100% observed precision (0/70 false positives). The lenient grader's recall is 97% against human labels. A keyword-anchored extraction pipeline raises the strict grader's recall by 60 percentage points over a last-number heuristic; the lenient grader is architecturally parser-independent. An iterative nudge mechanism raises grading run success from 36% to 97% and lenient-pass rates from 16% to 46%; comparing nudging with and without original-question re-injection shows that re-injection offers no benefit, confirming the nudge as an answer template cue. We further observe in this case study that variable type is the task metadata field most consistently associated with grading pipeline dynamics and observed outcome grades.
summary: this paper explores the challenges of evaluating agentic data analysis systems, which are ai agents that can perform complex tasks like generating code, numerical results, and verbal diagnostics. because their outputs are so rich and varied, it's hard to reliably assess their performance and distinguish genuine errors from issues in the grading process itself. the research investigates how automated graders perform and suggests strategies to improve their accuracy. as you delve into agents and genai, understanding robust evaluation methods is crucial for building reliable systems. a key takeaway is to design your evaluation metrics carefully, considering the multi-faceted nature of agentic outputs, and perhaps combine automated grading with human review for better accuracy.
why: helps you reliably evaluate complex agentic ai systems you might build.

title: AI Economist Agent: An Agentic Framework for Model-Grounded Economic Analysis with RAG, Knowledge Graphs, and Large Language Models
author: Masahiro Kato
raw_text: We propose a model-grounded RAG-based AI economist with an agentic framework for economic scenario analysis using large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs. While LLMs can generate fluent economic narratives, economists are often required to make economic claims grounded by economic theory and real-world data. Based on this motivation, this study proposes an RAG-based AI economist, which utilizes knowledge graphs including economic data and theory and LLM-based agents to plan the analysis, retrieve relevant evidence, select appropriate models, and generate reports. In our framework, we do not produce quantitative claims directly with the language model alone; instead, we generate narratives grounded in explicit model-based computations and linked to the retrieved evidence via AI agents. We refer to our framework as an AI economist agent. We evaluate the AI economist agent in two applications: economist report generation for U.S. inflation persistence and Federal Reserve policy, and bank stress-test narrative generation for U.S. commercial real estate refinancing stress. The results illustrate how grounding the generated reports improves their economic coherence and traceability.
summary: this paper introduces an 'ai economist' framework that combines retrieval-augmented generation (rag), knowledge graphs, and large language model (llm) agents for economic analysis. the main idea is to ensure that economic claims made by llms are always grounded in real economic theory and data, rather than just generating fluent but potentially inaccurate narratives. llm-based agents plan the analysis, while rag and knowledge graphs provide the necessary factual context and data. this work directly connects to your interests in rag, llms, and agents, showing how to build more reliable and fact-grounded ai applications. you could try exploring how to integrate external knowledge sources into your own llm projects to enhance their factual accuracy.
why: shows how rag and agents ground llms in real data for reliable analysis.
